claim: Qualcomm CEO Cristiano Amon disclosed that Apple-related chip revenue will fall roughly 50% sequentially between the September and December 2026 quarters, sooner and sharper than Qualcomm's own guidance had modeled, because industry-wide semiconductor supply constraints accelerated Apple's in-house C2 modem rollout.
stance_target: Forward margin effect of in-house modems (timing and scale)
scope_conditions: Qualcomm Q3 FY2026 earnings, Reuters interview July 29 2026
quoted_support: Apple-related chip revenue will fall roughly 50 percent sequentially between the September and December 2026 quarters -- a sharper drop than the company had modeled, arriving sooner than its own guidance suggested.

claim: Qualcomm's estimated iPhone 18 modem share, previously guided at roughly 20%, is now expected by Qualcomm's own CFO to be 'materially lower' than that figure.
stance_target: Forward margin effect of in-house modems (scale of Qualcomm displacement)
scope_conditions: Qualcomm Q3 FY2026 earnings call, CFO Akash Palkhiwala
quoted_support: Qualcomm had previously estimated it would supply modems for roughly 20 percent of the iPhone 18 lineup ... That figure is now off the table. CFO Akash Palkhiwala told analysts on the earnings call that the company's actual share in the upcoming iPhone launch will be 'materially lower' than the 20 percent estimate.

claim: For the iPhone 18 Pro, Apple is expected to deploy a dual-modem strategy: international units use Apple's own C2 modem, while US units retain a Qualcomm Snapdragon modem, because Apple's C-series does not yet match Qualcomm's mmWave (24-100 GHz) performance required for dense US urban 5G deployments by Verizon and AT&T.
stance_target: Forward margin effect of in-house modems (scale and completeness of displacement)
scope_conditions: iPhone 18 Pro, US vs. international markets, based on leaked supply-chain intelligence corroborated by multiple analysts as of mid-2026
quoted_support: international iPhone 18 Pro models will deploy the C2 while US models will retain a Qualcomm modem to preserve mmWave performance. ... Without matching Qualcomm's mmWave capability, Apple cannot universally deploy its own modem in the US Pro line without delivering a functionally inferior network experience.

claim: Apple's patent licensing agreement with Qualcomm (successor to the 2019 litigation settlement) runs through at least March 2027, meaning Qualcomm continues to collect licensing revenue from Apple even as chip/hardware revenue from Apple declines -- a bridge that softens but does not eliminate the revenue cliff.
stance_target: Whether Qualcomm displacement savings are fully retained by Apple as margin, or partly offset by ongoing payments
quoted_support: Qualcomm's patent licensing agreement with Apple -- the successor to the 2019 settlement that ended a years-long legal dispute -- runs through at least March 2027, continuing to generate licensing revenue from Apple even as chip revenue declines. That bridge softens the cliff but does not flatten it.

claim: The long-run strategic case for in-house modems is architectural, not just a per-unit royalty saving: once Apple integrates the C-series baseband onto the same die/package as the A-series application processor (as already done for Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and Ultra Wideband), it gains system-wide power/thermal optimization that a third-party modem supplier relationship structurally cannot replicate -- implying the margin/differentiation benefit compounds over time rather than being a one-off unit-cost reduction.
stance_target: Owning silicon is load-bearing for margin (durability argument)
scope_conditions: Forward-looking architectural claim; integration has not yet occurred as of the C1/C2 generation
quoted_support: Once Apple integrates the C-series baseband with the A-series SoC on a unified die or package ... it will be able to optimize power draw and thermal output across the full compute stack in ways that a third-party modem supplier relationship structurally cannot replicate. ... When it arrives, no price concession or technical specification will make a return to an external modem commercially rational for Apple.

claim: Qualcomm's handset chip business is materially impaired independent of the Apple displacement: QCT handset revenue fell to $5.09 billion in Q3 FY2026, down 20% year over year, with QCT gross margins falling below the historical 48-50% baseline range due to memory-price inflation pushing OEMs to lower-tier chips.
stance_target: Qualcomm's ability to absorb Apple modem revenue loss
quoted_support: QCT handset revenue fell to $5.09 billion in the quarter, down 20 percent year over year, weighed down by unprecedented memory price inflation that pushed original equipment manufacturers toward lower-tier chips and older inventory. QCT gross margins fell below Qualcomm's historical 48-to-50-percent baseline range as a result.

claim: Qualcomm is targeting non-handset revenue (automotive, IoT, data center) growth exceeding 60% in fiscal 2027, sufficient in management's own framing to fully replace lost Apple product revenue within the year, with automotive revenue already at a record $1.59 billion in Q3 FY2026 (+61% YoY) and a raised $7 billion automotive exit run-rate target.
stance_target: Whether Qualcomm's loss of Apple business is offset elsewhere (relevant to competitive dynamics, not directly to Apple's margin)
scope_conditions: Qualcomm Q3 FY2026 guidance and targets
quoted_support: combined non-handset revenue growth ... is forecast to exceed 60 percent in fiscal 2027, fully replacing Apple product revenue lost in fiscal 2026. ... QCT automotive revenue reached a record $1.59 billion in fiscal Q3 2026, up 61 percent year over year

claim: Apple's decision to build its own modem originated from the 2019 acquisition of Intel's smartphone modem division, taking six years to reach first shipment (C1 in the iPhone 16e, early 2025), indicating in-house silicon substitution for complex components carries multi-year development lead times, relevant to how quickly announced silicon strategies convert to realized margin.
stance_target: Timing of forward margin effect from in-house modems
quoted_support: Apple acquired Intel's smartphone modem division in 2019 and spent six years building internal baseband expertise and intellectual property before shipping its first in-house 5G modem (the C1) in the iPhone 16e in early 2025.
